newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians picnic at traditional desert festival.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians picnic at traditional desert festival.

text.p: Hundreds of Palestinian families, eager to escape political worries, have gathered at a West Bank desert site to picnic and watch dancing dervishes, keeping a tradition dating from the 13th Century.

Children queued for cotton candy and soft drinks on Friday outside a multi-domed complex tucked between the dunes of the Jordan Valley desert as their parents inspected the rooms inside or sat on blankets chatting and eating sandwiches.

Thousands packed the Nabi Mousa shrine, a fortress-like structure built in 1269 by the Mameluke Sultan Baybars for Moslems travelling from Jerusalem to venerate the biblical Moses, believed to be buried on Mount Nebo in nearby Jordan.

Just a few dozen kilometres (miles) from the festival, Palestinian protesters were clashing with Israeli troops in the West Bank towns of Bethlehem and Hebron on Friday for the 16th consecutive day over an Israeli settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Palestinians believe the festivities date back to the time of Moslem war hero Saladin, revered by Moslems as the man who liberated Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.
"We are here to celebrate a tradition that dates back to the times of Saladin," said Sheikh Mohammed al-Jamal, custodian of the shrine.
The month-long gatherings, called "The Prophet Moses Festival", were a big attraction for Palestinians during British rule in Palestine between 1918 and 1948.

According to local tradition, the festivities began under Saladin as a way of drawing Moslems out of Jerusalem to prevent friction with Christian pilgrims travelling to the Holy Land for the Easter holidays.
Elderly Palestinians attending Friday's opening recalled that celebrations used to attract more than half a million people from all over Palestine and neighbouring Arab countries.

"It used to be a very colourful occasion. People would gather at (Jerusalem's) al-Aqsa mosque and march with flags and camp out for a whole week," recalled Ahmed Ibrahim, 68, a Palestinian refugee who was displaced in 1948 and now lives in the West Bank.
He said that organisers would slaughter hundreds of sheep to feed the crowds amid horse racing, traditional dancing and Moslem teachings.
The festival lost its glamour after the 1948 division of Palestine between Israel and Jordan and has diminished in importance since the Jewish state occupied the West Bank in 1967.
The site, which Israel transferred to Palestinian management under a Palestinian self-rule deal, saw a revival of the ancient tradition on Friday.
A newly established Palestinian tourism committee decorated the courtyard of the 120-room building with pictures of President Yasser Arafat, coloured lights and national flags.
A police band played the Palestinian national anthem at the start of the ceremony, where Arafat representatives delivered speeches.
But only a few of the thousands of Palestinians who travelled from all over the West Bank and Israel sat to listen to the speeches.
Some shopped for cheap toys and local delicacies while others inspected the premises of the shrine. Others watched as a group of dervishes danced to the beat of drums while reciting Islamic songs.
Israeli soldiers stood guard on the overlooking hills.
"I brought my family here to enjoy a day out, meet people and mark a tradition," said Abdel-Rahim al-Nammari, a 68-year-old retired teacher from Jerusalem.
"Everybody knows that the prophet Moses's grave is not here. But this is just a historic symbol that brings people from all over Palestine together," he said.
